question: What is the meaning of eu ecolabel in relation to compliance and certification?
description: The EU Ecolabel is a certification that signifies compliance with specific environmental criteria set out by Regulation (EC) No 66/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council. It is a voluntary label that indicates a product's adherence to certain sustainability standards, such as durability, repairability, and recyclability.

The internationally recognized and accepted classification system for 
labels is issued by the ISO 14020 standard and categorizes labels into 
three types based on their verification (ISO, 2021b), self declarations 
(ISO, 2021a), and LCA data (ISO, 2021c). Eco-certificates and 
eco-labels frequently coincide, hence, the terms are often ’incor­
rectly’ used interchangeably to refer to the combination of concepts 
while concepts technically can exist independently. 
The key difference between certificates is that (1) an eco-certificate 
displays the environmental performance of a product on a static 
collected life cycle inventory while passport is a dynamic registration 
that takes place during the life cycle of a product, (2) not necessarily, but 
typically an eco-certificate is assigned to a product design, rather than a 
unique object, and (3) a passport attempts to valuate a product. 
3.6. Contents 
Passports appear in variants, for instance, with a focus on specific 
type of objects (e.g., buildings (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016), in­
frastructures (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018), clothing (Riedelsheimer et al., 
2020)) or with a specific purpose (e.g., renovation (Sesana et al., 2021), 
recycling (Spengler and Schr¨oter, 2003), optimizing operational use (Ye 
et al., 2020)). Passport requirements typically shape along with the 
intended product application. For example, a passport of a large com­
mercial company structure may not need the same level of detail as one 
for small residential buildings (Gonçalves et al., 2021; Transitieteam 
CBE, 2020; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018). Fig. 5 provides an overview of the 
attributes (lower level) that passports can typically consist of. This sup­
ports in deriving more holistic understanding of the typical components 
(higher-level) of a concept (bold text in Fig. 5 or see Fig. A4 and Table A6 
in Appendix A4). 
Nearly every passport contains a digital representation of the phys­
ical composition and technical characteristics of an object (C.12). 
Frequently reported data attributes are: information regarding the 
quality conditions of an object (C.1), the servicing history of an object 
(C.20), guidelines for maintenance, safety and recycling (C.13-C.18) and 
the valuation of an object (C.3). Performance indicators are also 
commonly part of a passport, but not all passports offer such metrics to 
measure the environmental performance of the object. EPDs and energy 
certificates are most frequently observed. Remarkable is the usual lack 
of circularity indicators (Moraga et al., 2019) reported while these align 
well with one of the key passport goals. A possible explanation is that 
sustainability and circularity indicators may introduce subjectivity both 
by focusing on specific aspects of sustainability or circularity and can 
apply weight to the objective results in selected indicator formula’s 
(Moraga et al., 2019). Moreover, for the sole purpose of identifying the 
value for use, recovery, and reuse, indicators may be helpful, but not 
always strictly required. There are two popular decision support attri­
butes in passports. Firstly, tools to explore options for recovery and 
renovation (C.49) which support object governance by letting users’ 
compare known alternative treatments. Secondly, scenario modelling 
(C.50) allows users to reason about unknown future states of the object 
which may help to identify a CE governance strategy. 
3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7).
